Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette:
Marisol Vega, a 57-year-old detective, traced the beginning of her problems to a raid on an illegal storage site two years earlier. She had gone in with other officers expecting drugs and weapons. Instead, when a drum was punctured, a harsh chemical cloud spread through the room. What she remembered most clearly was the sudden burn in her throat and chest, the panicked sense that no air was getting in, and the smell-sharp, clinical, almost like antiseptic layered over sweat trapped under body armor as officers crowded and shouted. She was pulled out coughing and gasping, later treated in the hospital, where the same sterilized smell hung in the hallways while uniformed personnel and supervisors spoke around her about protocol, exposure limits, and paperwork. Even now, what stayed with her was not a single coherent account but flashes: the sting in her lungs, a sleeve over someone's mouth, boots scraping concrete, the sensation that she was suffocating.

In the months afterward, those sensory fragments began to intrude into ordinary life. At work, if a suspect in an interview room smelled strongly of sweat, or if she walked past the hospital unit where injured officers were sometimes sent for clearance, her chest tightened and she felt short of breath in exactly the way she had during the exposure. In those moments the memory did not arrive as a story she could tell herself from beginning to end. It hit in disconnected pieces and with an immediacy that made her feel she was back inside that building. She would put her hands over her face, partly to block the smell and partly as if she could shut the whole thing out, and then force herself to think about something else-the details of another case, a grocery list, anything that might stop the memory before it fully formed.

She had also come to believe that the people and institutions who were supposed to protect her had failed her. She spoke bitterly about being sent into a hazardous scene without proper warning and about later being treated as a liability to be processed rather than a person who had nearly died. Around commanders, hospital staff, or anyone in uniform outside her immediate team, she became guarded and avoidant, finding reasons to leave, cutting conversations short, refusing optional briefings. The belief that she had been let down hardened into a broader conviction that she had to stay on guard all the time because no one else would keep her safe. That stance followed her everywhere: in the precinct she watched doorways, in restaurants she tracked exits, and at home she startled at unexpected bangs from the street, her body already braced before she had consciously registered the sound.

What frightened Marisol most was how flat and altered she felt. She said she could remember that she used to laugh easily with colleagues and call her adult son just to talk, but now she felt blunted, as if normal emotion had been sealed off. That loss seemed to confirm her fear that the exposure had changed her permanently. When a wave of breathlessness came, or she caught the antiseptic smell of cleaning supplies in the station hallway, it was not only frightening in itself; it also seemed like proof that she was still trapped in it and would never be normal again. The trigger became evidence for her worst conclusions, and those conclusions made her even more sensitive to the next smell, the next constriction in her chest, the next reminder that danger could appear without warning.

As this settled in, her habits tightened around it. She redirected her thoughts so quickly and so often that the memory remained broken, never fully linked into something finished and past. Because she pushed it away before it could unfold, the pieces returned uninvited-an image, a bodily sensation, a burst of panic-with the same present-tense force. Each time that happened, she read it as confirmation that she was still damaged and that vigilance was necessary. Covering her face, leaving meetings with supervisors, and mentally fleeing into other topics gave brief relief, but afterward she felt ashamed, more distant from coworkers, and more certain that she was no longer the detective she had been. Her lieutenant had noticed that she now avoided hospital-related assignments and became visibly tense when emergency alarms sounded in the building.

By the time she sought help, the strain was affecting both work and family. She was still showing up for duty, but only by exhausting herself through constant scanning and by steering around anything that smelled medical, humanly sweaty, or closed-in enough to make her notice her breathing. A recent case interview was what finally pushed her in: the witness arrived straight from a construction shift, smelling strongly of sweat, and Marisol suddenly felt she was back in the chemical cloud, hands over her face, unable to hear the questions being asked. She left the room and sat in her car shaking, convinced for a moment that she could not trust her own body or memory. She came to treatment afraid that if this continued she would lose her job and never feel like herself again, but also hoping, cautiously, that the event might one day feel over rather than as if it were still happening.
